en: A space launch vehicle is a rocket that carries satellites or space probes into space beyond Earth. Korea successfully launched Naro in 2013, but Naro's first-stage rocket was built in cooperation with Russia. So the Korea Aerospace Research Institute set a goal of completing the entire process—from design to production, testing, and launch operation—with domestic technology, and began developing Nuri, Korea's own space launch vehicle.

Nuri is a three-stage launch vehicle about 47 meters long. Its first stage bundles four 75-ton-class liquid engines together to produce powerful thrust, and the second and third stages separate one after another to carry the satellite up to its target altitude. There were many mountains to climb, such as the technology to bundle several engines and run them together and the technology to build huge fuel tanks, and many Korean companies took part in making parts and solved these problems together.

In its first launch in October 2021, Nuri failed to place a satellite model into the target orbit. However, the researchers found the cause and fixed it, and in the second launch in June 2022, Nuri safely placed a performance verification satellite into orbit. In the third launch in May 2023, it put several working satellites into orbit. With this, Korea became the seventh country in the world to launch a satellite weighing more than one ton with its own technology.

In May 2024, the Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA), a government agency in charge of space and aviation policy, opened its doors. KASA takes the role of leading both research and development and the growth of the industry. Space development is a comprehensive industry where technologies from many fields—machinery, electronics, and software—come together, so it is connected to a wide range of career paths. Because independence in launch vehicle technology is the starting point for moving on to satellite use and space exploration, Nuri's success is regarded as an event that opened a new chapter in Korea's space development.

en: The DNA inside a living thing's cells contains the genetic information needed for life. A gene is a unit of information that determines an organism's appearance and physical traits. "Genetic scissors" is a general term for technologies that find and cut a specific part of this DNA. Among them, CRISPR is a third-generation genetic scissors that appeared around 2012; because it is easier to make and costs less than earlier technologies, it changed the course of life science research around the world. The name CRISPR comes from a repeating DNA sequence structure discovered in bacteria.

The principle of CRISPR came from the immune system of bacteria. When a bacterium is infected by a virus, it records a piece of the virus's genes in its own DNA, and when the same virus invades again, it recognizes that part and cuts it. Scientists applied this principle and paired two elements: a guide RNA that leads the way to the target DNA, and the Cas9 protein that actually cuts that spot. Thanks to this, it became possible to select and cut a gene at the desired location.

Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna, who laid the foundation for this technology, received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020. CRISPR is widely used in research to uncover the causes of genetic diseases and to find treatments, and in 2023 a CRISPR-based treatment was approved for the first time in the world. This treatment is used to treat blood diseases caused by genetic abnormalities. In agriculture, CRISPR is used to develop crops that resist disease or are rich in nutrients.

Of course, there are also limits and controversies. Errors can occur in which the wrong part is cut instead of the target, and once a gene has been changed, it is hard to undo. In particular, editing the genes of reproductive cells, which are passed directly on to offspring, raises such serious ethical debate that many countries strictly regulate it. For CRISPR to benefit humanity, careful social agreement is needed as much as technological progress.

en: Artificial intelligence that answers questions as if having a conversation and writes texts on request is now widely used. AI that creates new results such as text, images, and sounds is called generative AI. Behind it lies a technology called the large language model. A model means something built to imitate a real-world process so that a computer can handle it. A language model is a program that calculates, using probability, in what order words are likely to follow one another.

A language model learns by reading vast amounts of text, such as books and internet documents. It repeats, countless times, the exercise of covering part of a sentence and guessing the word that comes next. This process of learning in advance is called pre-training. During this process, the countless parameters inside the model are adjusted little by little, and grammar, knowledge, and ways of expression soak into it. Once training is complete, when the model receives a question, it produces an answer by joining high-probability words one by one.

Generative AI helps with many kinds of work, from writing and translation to summarizing long texts and even writing computer programs. Many people also use it to refine their ideas or to study foreign languages. Because of this, the way people work is changing in many fields, including education, journalism, and industry. Still, one thing does not change: it remains a tool that supports human judgment.

However, its limits are also clear. A language model only produces plausible-sounding sentences based on probability; it cannot check for itself whether the content is true. This leads to the hallucination phenomenon, in which it states wrong information with confidence. There is also a risk that it learns and copies the biases contained in the texts it studied. In addition, it may not know about news that appeared after its training ended. This is why the habit of critically reviewing AI answers and checking their sources is so important.

en: Population structure is a framework that shows how a population is composed by age, gender, and other factors. It changes according to the number of people who are born, who die, and who move in or out. Korea is experiencing two phenomena at the same time: low birth rates, in which fewer babies are being born, and population aging, in which the share of elderly people in the total population is rising. According to surveys by the Ministry of Data and Statistics, these trends have continued steadily over many years.

In general, a society is called an aging society when people aged 65 or older make up more than 7% of the population, an aged society when they exceed 14%, and a super-aged society when they exceed 20%. Korea has recently entered the stage of a super-aged society, and the speed of this change is very fast even by world standards. As average life expectancy grows longer and the number of newborns falls, the shape of the population pyramid is also changing into a form that is narrow at the bottom and wide at the top.

Changes in population structure affect many areas of society. When the number of students falls, schools and the education system are adjusted, and when the working-age population that can hold jobs shrinks, companies find it harder to secure workers. On the other hand, demand for medical and care services grows, and the silver industry, which serves elderly people as its main customers, expands. How to run systems that generations pay for together, such as pensions and health insurance, is also being discussed again. In some regions, the population is shrinking and the vitality of local communities is weakening.

In response, the government is acting with a variety of policies. Typical examples are support systems that create a good environment for having and raising children, and programs that help elderly people with jobs and health. Because population change appears gradually over a long period, it is important to prepare in advance on the basis of accurate statistics. Understanding population structure is a starting point for looking ahead to the future of our society.

en: The overall level of the prices of goods and services traded in the market is called the price level. The price level is not the cost of one individual product; it combines the prices of many products to show an average trend. The Consumer Price Index that appears in the news is an indicator that expresses the movement of prices as a number. The phenomenon of prices rising continuously is called inflation, and when it occurs, the value of money falls relatively. This is because the amount of goods that can be bought with the same money decreases.

The basic principle behind price movement is supply and demand. When the demand to buy a product is greater than its supply, the price rises, and when supply is greater than demand, the price falls. Prices can also rise when the costs of making a product, such as raw material prices or wages, go up. When these factors appear across many products, the overall price level moves.

If prices rise or fall too quickly, the whole economy becomes unstable. That is why the Bank of Korea, the country's central bank, takes price stability as its most important goal. The Bank of Korea raises or lowers the base interest rate to influence the amount of money circulating in the market. When interest rates rise, consumption and investment decrease, which can have the effect of calming price increases. Conversely, when the economy slows down too much, the bank may lower interest rates to stimulate economic activity.

Meanwhile, the wages that working people receive have a lower limit set by law. The minimum wage system is designed to guarantee a minimum level of wages and protect low-paid workers. The minimum wage is deliberated and decided every year by the Minimum Wage Commission, in which members representing workers, members representing employers, and members representing the public interest take part. The commission considers a range of factors, such as workers' cost of living, the wages of similar workers, and labor productivity, and once the government confirms and officially announces the decision, it applies the following year.

en: Every year, a large amount of plastic waste flows into the sea. Much of it comes from land. Trash thrown away on the streets travels with rainwater and rivers until it reaches the sea, and nets and buoys thrown away or lost during fishing also remain in the ocean. Trash floating on the sea sometimes travels far offshore along ocean currents. Plastic is convenient because it is light and strong, but it is a material that takes a very long time to break down in nature.

Plastic that enters the sea is gradually broken into small pieces by the action of waves, ultraviolet rays from sunlight, and salt. Pieces that have become smaller than 5 millimeters across are called microplastics. Microplastics may be particles made small from the start, or fragments created when larger plastics break apart. Because they are so small, they spread widely through the water and are very hard to remove. Such tiny pieces are found not only in seawater but also in mudflats and on sandy beaches.

Plastic waste causes many kinds of harm to the marine ecosystem. When seabirds and turtles mistake plastic for food and swallow it, their digestive organs can become blocked, and animals caught in abandoned nets sometimes lose their lives because they cannot move. Microplastics have been confirmed to move along the food chain, from plankton to fish, so scientists are continuing to study their effects. The coastal scenery is also damaged, hurting tourism and fishing.

Responses are being made on several levels. The government and the Korea Marine Environment Management Corporation collect trash from beaches and the sea and run programs to reduce fishing waste. The international community is discussing an agreement to reduce plastic pollution. Individual efforts, such as using fewer disposable products and sorting waste for recycling, are also important. The surest way to reduce the plastic heading to the sea is to produce less waste in the first place.

en: Gases in the atmosphere such as carbon dioxide and methane trap heat rising from the Earth's surface and keep the planet's temperature stable. This is called the greenhouse effect, and such gases are called greenhouse gases. The greenhouse effect itself is a natural phenomenon that is essential for life. However, fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and natural gas release carbon dioxide when they are burned. Since industrialization, the use of fossil fuels has increased greatly, raising the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, and the Earth's average temperature has risen along with it.

To respond to climate change, the international community signed the Paris Agreement and promised to keep the rise in the Earth's average temperature below a certain level. The goal set for this purpose is carbon neutrality. Carbon neutrality means reducing greenhouse gas emissions as much as possible and offsetting the remaining emissions through absorption by forests or storage technology, so that net emissions become zero. Many countries, including Korea, have declared carbon neutrality as their goal.

The key means is energy transition. Renewable energy comes from sources that nature supplies continuously and that never run out, such as sunlight, wind, and water. Solar power uses the principle that solar cells made of semiconductors produce an electric current when light falls on them. In wind power, the wind turns large blades, and a generator converts that rotation into electricity. Because no fuel is burned, almost no greenhouse gases are released while the electricity is being generated.

Still, the challenges are clear. Renewable energy is intermittent, meaning its output changes with the weather, so devices that store electricity and improvements to the power grid are needed. The large amount of land and money needed for power facilities, and consultation with local residents, are also important issues. That is why technologies that use energy efficiently and habits of saving energy are emphasized together. Improving the insulation of old buildings also helps save energy. Carbon neutrality is a goal that can be reached only when technology, institutions, and citizens' actions work together.

배출을 최대한 줄이되 남은 배출은 흡수와 저장으로 상쇄해 '실질적인' 배출을 0으로 만드는 것이다.
challenge.explain: 2문단에서 탄소중립은 배출량을 최대한 줄이고, 남은 배출량은 숲의 흡수나 저장 기술로 상쇄해 실질적인 배출을 0으로 만드는 것이라고 정의했다. 따라서 배출을 '완전히 없애는' 것과는 다르다. 온실효과가 생명에 필요한 자연 현상이라는 말은 1문단에 있지만, 그것이 배출을 줄일 필요가 없다는 근거는 될 수 없으므로 첫 번째 선지는 틀렸다.

en: The Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty is a vast collection of history books that organizes the records of the reigns of Joseon kings. At its foundation was the court historian system. Historians attended meetings between the king and his officials and wrote down the king's words and actions, along with affairs of the state large and small, in records called sacho. Because the principle that even the king could not freely read the sacho was upheld, historians could record the facts without worrying about those in power.

The Veritable Records were not compiled while a king was still alive. Only after a king died was a temporary office called the Sillokcheong set up and compilation begun. Its officials gathered and reviewed the sacho and documents from each government office, arranged them in order of time, and completed the records. When the compilation was finished, the sacho were washed in water to erase the writing, a practice called secho. This was done to prevent the contents of the records from leaking out and causing conflict.

Several copies of the completed records were made and stored separately in archives called sago. Even if the records in one archive were destroyed by fire or war, the copies elsewhere would survive. In fact, during the Japanese invasions of Korea in the 1590s, most of the archives burned down, but the copy at the Jeonju archive alone survived. After the war, Joseon made several new copies based on the surviving records and moved the archives deep into the mountains, where access was difficult, to keep them even safer.

The Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty cover the history of one dynasty over several hundred years almost without gaps. They record not only politics and diplomacy but also weather, astronomical events, and the daily lives of the people, making them precious material for historical research. In recognition of this value, the records were inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 1997. Today the records have been translated into modern Korean, and anyone can look them up on the internet. The spirit of record-keeping that protected five hundred years of Joseon history still lives on.

en: In 1443, King Sejong the Great created a new writing system called Hunminjeongeum, and in 1446 he proclaimed it to the people. Hunminjeongeum means "the correct sounds for teaching the people." At the time, there were no Korean letters for writing the Korean language, so people borrowed Chinese characters, but these were hard to learn and difficult for ordinary people to use. King Sejong wanted to create letters that anyone could easily learn and use, in order to ease the hardship of people who could not put into writing what they wished to say.

The consonants of Hunminjeongeum were created on the principle of imitating shapes. The five basic consonants copy the shapes of the speech organs as each sound is made. The letter ㄱ imitates the shape of the root of the tongue blocking the throat, and ㄴ the shape of the tongue touching the upper gums. The letter ㅁ came from the shape of the mouth, ㅅ from the shape of a tooth, and ㅇ from the shape of the throat. The remaining consonants were made by the principle of adding strokes to the basic letters. Since strokes are added as the sound becomes stronger, you can guess the nature of a sound just by looking at the shape of the letter.

The vowels begin from three basic letters that stand for heaven, earth, and human. The round dot ㆍ symbolizes heaven, the horizontal line ㅡ the flat earth, and the vertical line ㅣ a standing person. By combining these basic letters with one another, many vowels such as ㅏ and ㅗ were created in a systematic way. This method of writing countless sounds by combining a small number of basic letters according to fixed rules is highly efficient.

When Hunminjeongeum was created, it had twenty-eight letters in all: seventeen consonants and eleven vowels. Today, 24 of them are in use. The purpose and principles behind the letters are explained in detail in a book called the Hunminjeongeum Haerye, the explanatory edition. It is rare anywhere in the world for records to remain showing who created a writing system, when, and on what principles. In recognition of this value, the Hunminjeongeum Haerye was inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 1997.

en: Webtoons are digital comics that developed to fit the internet environment. They began to grow in earnest in the early 2000s, when Korean internet portals started serializing comics for free. At a time when the print comics market was struggling, webtoons opened a way to meet readers in a new space, the internet. Because anyone could access them easily, the readership expanded quickly, and the culture of communicating with readers through comments also added to the popularity of webtoons.

The most distinctive feature of the webtoon format is vertical scrolling. Unlike paper comics, which are read by turning pages, webtoons are read by scrolling down the screen. This style suits smartphone screens well, so people can read comfortably even while on the move. New storytelling techniques that make use of this vertical flow have also developed, such as adjusting the blank space between panels to express the passage of time or a feeling of tension.

Webtoons gradually formed an industrial ecosystem of their own. A partial-payment model, in which readers pay a fee to read some episodes in advance, took hold and created a stable revenue structure. Beyond authors and platforms, many other participants appeared, such as agencies that support authors and production studios where the writing and the drawing are handled by different people. Before a single webtoon is created and reaches its readers, many different jobs work together.

A webtoon's story does not stay inside the webtoon alone. Popular works are remade into dramas, films, games, and more. This spreading of an original story into many fields is called the expansion of intellectual property, or IP. Korean webtoon platforms have also expanded their services into many languages and gained readers overseas. The vertical-scroll format that took root in Korea has now become one of the standard formats for digital comics in many countries around the world.

en: Space is filled with high-energy particles that fly in from the Sun and from the distant universe. These are called space radiation. On Earth, the thick atmosphere and the magnetic field act as shields, so people live without serious harm. The Moon, however, has almost no atmosphere and only a very weak magnetic field, so space radiation pours straight down onto its surface.

Space radiation can damage the cells of the human body, so astronauts must prepare for it before staying on the Moon for a long time. That requires accurate data showing how strong the radiation on the lunar surface actually is and what kinds of particles arrive in what amounts. Only with accurate data can we decide how to build spacesuits and lunar bases. Data from the Moon's south pole, which many countries are watching as a candidate site for future crewed exploration, is especially important.

The lunar surface space radiation detector LVRAD, which is being developed under the leadership of the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute, is the instrument in charge of this task. It consists of a device that measures the amount and energy distribution of radiation and a device that measures neutrons. In August 2026, the Korea AeroSpace Administration signed an implementing arrangement with the U.S. National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) to send the detector on a lunar lander built by an American private company.

According to the plan, the detector will finish development by 2027 and then be moved to the United States, and it will head for the Moon's south pole aboard a lander launching in 2030. However, the launch date may change depending on NASA's schedule. The observation data gathered there will be used to study how space radiation affects the human body and to prepare for future crewed lunar exploration. It is also a chance for Korea to take on a role in international lunar exploration and show the world the level of its space science.

challenge.q: 이 글의 원리를 바탕으로, '대기가 지구보다 훨씬 얇고 자기장도 거의 없는 어떤 천체'에 대해 판단한 내용으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 대기가 조금이라도 있다면 방패 역할은 충분하므로, 그 천체에서도 사람들이 큰 피해 없이 살아갈 수 있을 것이다.
우주방사선은 태양에서만 날아오므로, 태양에서 멀리 떨어진 천체라면 방사선을 걱정할 필요가 없을 것이다.
사람이 그 천체에 오래 머물더라도, 우주복이나 기지를 설계할 때 방사선 자료는 따로 필요하지 않을 것이다.
대기와 자기장의 보호가 약하므로, 그 천체의 표면에는 지구 표면보다 강한 우주방사선이 내리쬘 것이다.
challenge.explain: 0문단에서 지구는 두꺼운 대기와 자기장이 방패 역할을 해 주고, 달은 대기가 거의 없고 자기장이 약해 방사선이 그대로 내리쬔다고 했습니다. 이 원리를 적용하면 보호막이 약한 천체의 표면에는 지구보다 강한 방사선이 도달할 것입니다. '방패'라는 본문 표현을 그대로 쓴 첫 번째 선지가 헷갈리지만, 본문은 '두꺼운' 대기가 막아 준다고 했으므로 얇은 대기만으로 충분하다고 볼 근거가 없고, 방사선은 태양뿐 아니라 먼 우주에서도 날아온다고 했으므로 두 번째 선지도 어긋납니다.

challenge.q: 이 글에 제시된 계획을 비판적으로 검토한 내용으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: LVRAD에는 중성자를 재는 장치가 빠져 있으므로, 달 표면의 방사선을 온전히 측정하기 어렵다.
달 남극의 방사선 자료는 이미 충분히 쌓여 있으므로, 새로 측정기를 보내는 것은 낭비에 가깝다.
발사 시기가 NASA의 일정에 달려 있으므로, 2030년에 달 남극에 도착한다는 계획은 미뤄질 가능성을 염두에 두어야 한다.
측정기 개발은 2027년에야 끝나므로, 2026년에 미리 이행약정을 맺은 것은 순서가 뒤바뀐 일이다.
challenge.explain: 3문단에서 발사 시기는 NASA의 일정에 따라 바뀔 수 있다고 명시했으므로, 2030년 도착이 늦어질 가능성을 고려하는 것이 타당한 비판적 검토입니다. 본문의 연도를 그대로 쓴 네 번째 선지가 헷갈리지만, 약정을 먼저 맺고 개발을 마치는 순서가 문제라는 근거는 본문 어디에도 없습니다. 첫 번째 선지는 LVRAD가 중성자를 측정하는 장치를 갖추고 있다는 2문단 내용과 어긋납니다.

en: The main cause of climate change is the greenhouse gases released when fossil fuels such as coal and oil are burned. The problem is that if companies can release greenhouse gases for free, they have no reason to spend money on reducing their emissions. So many countries have devised a way to put a price on pollution. Policies that make emitters pay for their carbon emissions are broadly called "carbon pricing." A leading example of such a policy is the greenhouse gas emissions trading scheme.

The emissions trading scheme rests on two pillars: a cap on total emissions and trading. First, the government sets the total amount of greenhouse gases that can be emitted across the whole country. Within that limit, it distributes emission allowances to companies. One unit of allowance is the right to emit one ton of greenhouse gases. In principle, a company can emit only as much greenhouse gas as the allowances it holds.

The key point is that allowances can be bought and sold in a market. A company that invests in technology to reduce greenhouse gases and has allowances left over can sell them and make a profit. In contrast, a company that runs short of allowances must buy them from the market. The higher the price of allowances rises, the more advantageous it becomes to cut one's own emissions rather than to buy. The system was designed so that reducing pollution literally pays.

Korea has been operating an emissions trading scheme since 2015, and allowances are traded on the Korea Exchange like stocks. The scheme covers more than 70% of the country's total greenhouse gas emissions, and about 770 companies are taking part in the fourth planning period, which began in 2026. Allowance prices move with the economy and with policy, and recently they have also swung sharply. Following the signals the price sends, companies draw up their plans for reducing emissions.

challenge.q:
윗글의 원리를 다음 상황에 적용한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
[상황] ㄱ기업은 온실가스 1톤을 줄이는 데 1만 원이 들고, ㄴ기업은 1톤을 줄이는 데 5만 원이 든다. 배출권은 시장에서 1톤에 3만 원에 거래되고 있다.
choices: ㄴ기업은 배출권을 사는 것보다 스스로 감축하는 편이 돈이 덜 든다.
ㄱ기업은 감축하지 말고 배출권을 사서 지금처럼 배출하는 편이 유리하다.

배출권 가격이 3만 원인 한, 두 기업 모두 굳이 비용을 들여 배출을 줄일 이유가 없다.
challenge.explain: ㄱ기업은 1만 원을 들여 1톤을 줄이고 남은 배출권을 3만 원에 팔면 이익이므로 스스로 감축하는 쪽이, ㄴ기업은 5만 원을 들여 줄이는 것보다 3만 원에 사 오는 쪽이 유리하다. 이것이 2문단의 '오염을 줄이는 일이 곧 돈이 되도록 만든' 원리다. 첫 번째 선지는 ㄴ기업의 감축 비용(5만 원)이 배출권 가격(3만 원)보다 높다는 점에서 틀렸고, 네 번째 선지는 배출에 값을 치르게 되면 ㄱ기업처럼 감축이 오히려 이익이 되는 기업이 생긴다는 글의 내용과 어긋난다.

en: Just as there are heatwaves on land, there are heatwaves in the sea. A 'marine heatwave' is a period in which the sea water stays much warmer than the normal level for that region and season for five days or more. Scientists usually use a standard: the water temperature must be high enough to fall in the top 10% of the normal distribution for that place and season. Because sea water holds heat longer than air, a marine heatwave, once it starts, can sometimes continue for weeks.

According to an analysis released by the Korea Meteorological Administration in August 2026, marine heatwaves occurred in the seas around Korea for an average of 83.3 days per year during the last ten years (2016-2025). That is 3.7 times the normal level. During the same period, the sea surface temperature was also 0.7 degrees higher than normal. The KMA expects that if warming continues, marine heatwaves will become more frequent and stronger, and by the end of the century most days of the year could be marine heatwave days.

When the sea gets hotter, the effects spread both inside and outside the ocean. Fish species that live in cold water move north, changing the kinds of fish that are caught, and fish on farms die in large numbers because they cannot stand the high water temperature. A hot sea also supplies the air with a great deal of heat and water vapor, which fuels heatwaves and heavy rain and makes typhoons stronger. The changes in the sea come back to us as the weather on land.

So scientists watch the water temperature in real time with satellites and observation equipment at sea, and when it rises sharply, they issue warnings so that fishing communities can prepare. Cutting greenhouse gas emissions can also slow down the warming of the ocean. For marine scientists and climate researchers who study marine heatwaves, and for people in the fishing industry who look for ways to adapt to a changed sea, the warming ocean is becoming a stage for new careers.

en: Colorectal cancer can be treated well when it is found early. But colonoscopy, the main screening test, requires a hard preparation process to empty the bowel, and the simple stool test has limits in accuracy. So many people put off getting screened. Recently, a new possibility was suggested to lower this barrier: a test that screens for the risk of colorectal cancer with just one blood draw.

When cells in our body die or break apart, they release small pieces of DNA into the blood. These floating pieces are called 'cell-free DNA.' The pieces released by cancer cells are slightly different from those of normal cells in their length, their end structures, and where they sit in the genome. In other words, they are traces that cancer cells leave in the blood. A test that reads the state of the body from fluids like blood is called a 'liquid biopsy.'

The problem is that these differences are too small for human eyes to pick out. This is where artificial intelligence shows its power. In August 2026, a research team at Asan Medical Center announced the results of a study that used AI to analyze blood data from 1,677 people, including colorectal cancer patients and healthy people. The sensitivity for finding cancer patients was 90.4%, and the specificity for correctly identifying healthy people was 94.7%. The test also kept high performance for early-stage cancer.

What would change if testing became easier? If a simple blood draw could screen for risk, people who have been putting off screening would get tested earlier, and there would be more chances to find cancer at an early stage. However, this is only a screening test that filters out the possibility of cancer. To confirm a diagnosis, a colonoscopy and a biopsy are still needed, and the test must pass more verification before it is used in real screening programs.

Research like this is completed through the cooperation of many experts: doctors who treat patients and collect data, life scientists who study the features of cell-free DNA, and medical AI developers who build models that learn patterns. Whether you are interested in medicine, life science, or artificial intelligence, this field keeps a door open where they all meet.

en: In the heart of Seoul stand two UNESCO World Heritage sites. One is Changdeokgung, a palace of the Joseon dynasty, listed in 1997. The other is Jongmyo, the shrine that holds the spirit tablets of Joseon's kings and queens, listed in 1995. Wooden pillars and tiled roofs catch the eye first, but beneath them thousands of stones form the platforms, stairs, and walls that hold the buildings up.

Since 2023, the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage of the Korea Heritage Service has been carrying out a project to study these stones scientifically. Researchers examined all 4,421 stones one by one — 2,922 at Changdeokgung and 1,499 at Jongmyo — and identified what kind of rock each one is. They then marked the results in color on drawings of the buildings, creating 'rock maps' that were shared with the public.

The survey showed that most of the stones are pale pink granite. More than 90% of the stones at Changdeokgung and over 99% at Jongmyo are this rock. The same pale pink granite is found on mountains around Seoul, such as Inwangsan, Ansan, Bukaksan, and Bukhansan. This suggests that the builders may have brought the stones from mountains not far away.

Why does it matter where the stones came from? Stone looks strong, but over many years it weathers, cracks, and breaks off. If a damaged stone is replaced with one from a different source, the color and texture will not match, and it may weather at a different speed, spoiling the look of the heritage site. That is why the survey also compared granite from the Seoul and Pocheon areas. The data will serve as basic material for choosing stones for future repair and restoration.

This survey brought together petrology, the study of rocks, and conservation science, which protects cultural heritage. Conservation scientists use knowledge from chemistry, geology, and biology to analyze what heritage objects are made of and how damaged they are, and to find ways to treat them. It is a fitting career for someone who loves old things and scientific inquiry at the same time.

en: Electricity is invisible, but it is a product that costs more the farther it travels. As it flows through power lines, some of it is lost as heat, and building and managing the transmission network also costs a great deal of money. In Korea, however, nuclear power plants and renewable energy facilities are concentrated in the southern regions, while the factories and data centers that use a lot of electricity are concentrated in the capital area. The places that make electricity and the places that use it are far apart.

On August 26, 2026, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment and the Korea Electric Power Corporation held a public hearing and unveiled a draft design for a regional electricity pricing system for industry. By adding a new 'regional adjustment rate' to the current bill, the plan divides the country into eleven regions and applies different industrial rates to each. In the southern regions, which are close to power plants, rates would fall by up to 18 won per kilowatt-hour, about 10% of the average industrial price. Jeju, as an island with special conditions, was left out of this plan.

In economics, a price is a signal. If rates differ by region, companies that use a lot of electricity will consider cheaper regions when they build factories or data centers. The government hopes this signal will spread industrial facilities away from the capital area, cutting transmission costs and boosting local economies.

Of course, there are open questions. When companies choose a location, they weigh many conditions besides electricity rates, such as workers, transportation, and distance to business partners, so some point out that a rate gap alone may not actually move factories. Others worry that regions may clash over gains and losses. The plan is not a finished system yet; it is a draft that will be revised based on opinions gathered at the hearing.

This news connects to many careers. Engineers who design transmission networks and power systems, business experts who calculate rates and locations to shape company strategy, and policy experts who turn rate systems into laws and rules all work on top of this design. Reading the signal called price is a tool they all share.

en: On August 27, 2026, Korea's Ministry of Education announced that classroom teachers will lead the development of textbooks and learning materials for the new artificial intelligence (AI) subjects taught in schools. Through an open call, sixteen subjects were selected: six for elementary school, two for middle school, and eight for high school. This is the first time the government has supported textbook development for AI subjects.

Korean textbooks are divided into three types according to how they are developed. Government-designated textbooks are written directly by the state. Authorized textbooks are made by publishers and must pass a national screening. Approved textbooks are reviewed and approved by provincial offices of education so that schools can use them; their procedures are relatively flexible, which suits newly created subjects well. The new AI textbooks will be developed as approved textbooks.

Until now, many schools offered AI-related classes without official textbooks, so teachers had to create their own materials every semester, which was a heavy burden. In this project, classroom teachers join as authors and lead the whole process, from analyzing the curriculum and organizing units to writing the manuscript. Their real experience of teaching students goes straight into the textbook.

The plan also reflects how fast AI technology changes. The main textbook will contain core concepts and principles that last a long time, while the latest technology trends and hands-on examples will be made as separate booklets or web-based materials that are updated continuously. The finished textbooks will be tried out in schools in the first semester of 2027 and, after review and approval by provincial offices of education, used in classes from March 2028.

The main characters of this change are today's students, because they will be the first generation to learn AI with these new textbooks. If teaching attracts you, you can dream of becoming a teacher; if you want to support learning with technology, an edtech developer; if you like explaining knowledge in a simple way, an educational content creator. Knowing how textbooks are made is the first step.

en: A work of art begins to change the moment it is finished. Pigments lose their brightness, paper oxidizes and turns yellow, and cracks appear on the surface. The activity of slowing this damage and extending the life of a work is called conservation science. Because it demands both a knowledge of art history and the chemistry needed to analyze materials, conservation science sits on the border between art and science.

Korea's National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art is the country's only national institution devoted to art conservation. It divides the work into four fields, paper, oil painting, sculpture and craft, and material analysis, and looks after some 8,000 works. A conservator does not touch a piece right away. A condition survey comes first, recording where and how badly the work is damaged, and that record becomes the basis for deciding how to treat it. Leaving a reason behind matters more than the treatment itself.

In practice, the larger share of conservation is not repair but prevention. The museum keeps galleries and storage rooms at 18 to 22 degrees and holds relative humidity between 50 and 70 percent. Too much moisture invites mold, and too little makes surfaces crack. Lighting also differs by material. Oil paintings are limited to 150 lux or less, ink and watercolor paintings to 100 lux, and dyed works and prints to 80 lux. Metal and stone, which resist light well, may be shown at up to 1,500 lux.

Contemporary art makes conservation harder still. Nam June Paik's The More, the Better is a tower of 1,003 cathode ray tube monitors rising 18.5 meters. When it was shut down in 2018 because of age, the museum spent three years restoring it. Seven hundred and thirty-seven damaged monitors were repaired with secondhand parts, and 266 that could no longer be used kept their outer shells while flat panels replaced the inside. Preserve the original form, or preserve the ability to run? A conservator has to choose, again and again.

en: Pansori is a traditional Korean performing art. One singer tells a long story. A drummer marks the rhythm beside the singer. The word joins pan, meaning a gathering place, and sori, meaning sound. The pan is not only the stage. A singer, a drummer, and an audience must all gather before a pan truly exists.

The singer moves among three ways of telling. Chang is sung melody. Aniri is plain speech that explains the scene and carries the dialogue. Ballim is gesture, shown with a fan in hand. There is no scenery and only one performer, yet the story may hold dozens of characters and run for hours.

The rhythm sets the speed of the story. Jinyangjo is the slowest. Jungmori, jungjungmori, and jajinmori follow. Hwimori is the fastest. Slow patterns stretch out sorrow, and fast ones drive a chase. The drummer marks these patterns and controls how the sound speeds up or slows down. An old saying names the drummer first and the singer second.

The audience holds an unusual place. People answer the sound with short cries of praise. The word for these cries means a sound that lifts someone up. It tells the singer she is doing well, and it is also a way of joining in. In many shows the stage and the seats are clearly divided, but here the listeners help build the pan.

Pansori once had twelve stories. As each grew longer, five remained: Chunhyangga, Simcheongga, Heungboga, Sugungga, and Jeokbyeokga. Korea named pansori a national intangible heritage in 1964. UNESCO chose it as a masterpiece of oral heritage in 2003, and it entered the representative list in 2008.

en: In 2024 the novelist Han Kang received the Nobel Prize in Literature, the first Korean writer to do so. The judges of that prize, however, cannot read Korean. What they read was the work in English and in Swedish. Before a work can cross a border, someone has to write it again in another language. That person is the translator.

Han Kang's novel The Vegetarian was carried into English by Deborah Smith, a British translator. She studied English literature at Cambridge and began learning Korean in 2010. It was a deliberate choice, made because almost no Korean literature was reaching English readers. In 2012, in her third year of study, she began to translate the novel.

Smith's work did not stop at translation. She first rendered about twenty pages and sent them to a British publisher with a proposal to publish. The editor accepted. Once the book appeared, she also took on the task of writing to critics and readers about it. In 2016 the book won the Booker Prize International, and the writer and the translator were honoured together.

The hardest problem in translation is a word with no counterpart. Words such as soju, seonsaengnim, and hyeong carry the relationships and habits of a society inside them. The moment they are swapped for a similar English word, that texture is gone. Smith chose not to translate such words and kept the Korean sounds instead.

This choice shows that translation is not mere substitution. A translator moves words and at the same time decides what to keep and what to change. A word left as it is feels strange to the reader, and that very strangeness becomes a passage into another culture. This is why a translator is called a bridge between two languages.

en: For a long time Joseon landscape painting followed picture books from China. The painter had never been to China, yet Chinese mountains and rivers filled the paper. An ideal landscape was already set down in those books, and painters followed the pattern. Such work is called idea landscape. There were many fine paintings, but the land of Korea was not in them.

Jeong Seon changed this practice. He climbed Geumgangsan and walked every corner of Inwangsan many times over. Then he painted the scenery his own eyes had confirmed. A landscape that takes a real place as its subject is called jingyeong, a true view. From this time the land of Korea became the subject of the picture.

In 1751, at seventy-six, Jeong Seon painted Inwangsan after a shower had passed. The work is Inwangjesaekdo. He pressed dark ink onto rocks the rain had turned black, and white cloud is lifting from the slope. The painting stayed in private hands for a long time. In 2021 the family of the late chairman Lee Kun-hee gave it to the National Museum of Korea, and it became a painting anyone can see.

Yet treating a true view as a photograph leads to a mistake. Geumgangjeondo, painted in 1734, shows the point. You cannot stand in one place and take in all the peaks of the inner Geumgang at once. Jeong Seon walked from Jangansa up to Birobong, then rebuilt what he had seen from a viewpoint looking down from above and set it inside a single circle. It is a picture seen from a position that does not exist.

This is not a failure but a method. The painter does not move what enters the eye straight onto the paper. He judges what to keep and what to gather. The word jingyeong means the scene before one's eyes and also the true form of that scene. What Jeong Seon looked for was not the surface of Inwangsan but the weight of a mountain soaked with rain.

en: In 1794 King Jeongjo began building a new fortress at Suwon. This fortress is Hwaseong. It was a large civil engineering project for the time and demanded enormous funds and skill. Jeong Yak-yong designed a lifting device for heavy materials and a sturdy cart, and these reduced both labour and cost. The fortress was completed in 1796.

When the work was done, the king had the entire process set down as a record. The book made in this way is the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe. It carries drawings of the walls and the attached buildings, the kind and quantity of materials, the names of the craftsmen and labourers, the wages paid to them, and a daily log of the work. It was printed in 1801 and appeared as ten volumes.

Almost two hundred years then passed. Through the colonial period and the Korean War the walls and buildings of Hwaseong fell into serious ruin. When restoration began in the 1970s, the most important source was the Uigwe. Because the drawings, the measurements, and the list of materials survived, the ruined parts could be rebuilt close to their original form.

There is a reason this matters. A principle holds that restoring cultural heritage requires firm evidence, and that work must stop at the point where evidence runs out and guesswork begins. For that reason a heavily rebuilt structure is usually hard to recognise as World Heritage. There is no way to confirm what the original form was. Hwaseong was different on exactly this point.

In 1997 Hwaseong was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list. In 2007 the royal protocols of the Joseon dynasty, including the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe, entered the Memory of the World register. The fortress and the book that described it were recognised side by side. A record does not merely write down what has passed. It also settles what can be brought back long afterwards.

en: Learning something new does not turn it into a lasting memory right away. New information is first stored for a time in a part of the brain called the hippocampus. A memory at this stage is unstable, so it fades easily or is pushed aside by other memories. Something crammed just before a test, and gone a few days later, is an example.

The process by which an unstable short-term memory becomes a long-term one is called consolidation. At its core, consolidation is a move. Information held for a time in the hippocampus gradually shifts to the wide storage space of the cerebral cortex. And this move takes place mostly while we are asleep.

A sleeping brain is not a resting brain. Patterns of nerve activity that appeared during learning are repeated while we sleep, in a form compressed in time. Researchers call this memory reactivation and regard it as the central mechanism of consolidation. The repetition is most marked during slow-wave sleep, the deepest stage.

So what happens if sleep is cut short? Many studies have confirmed that restricting sleep after new learning seriously impairs consolidation. When material memorised through an all-nighter does not last, the reason is not willpower or concentration. It is biological.

The national mental health portal advises nine to ten hours of sleep a day for children and teenagers. How much a person needs, however, differs from person to person, and the minimum for each is the amount that lets them get through the next day without fatigue. Closing the book is not the end of studying. That is what sleep research tells us.

en: For a long time a criminal trial was the work of judges who had studied law for years. In Korea, however, there is also the citizen participation trial, in which ordinary citizens take part as jurors. After watching the arguments in the courtroom from beginning to end, the jurors give their judgment on whether the defendant is guilty. When they find guilt, they also give their opinion on what punishment would be fitting.

Jurors are not volunteers. From a list of candidates prepared in advance the court draws as many as it needs at random and calls them to a selection hearing. Any citizen over the age of twenty may serve without special qualification, but people in certain jobs, such as lawyers and police officers, are excluded. The list is remade each year by the chief district judge, drawn at random from resident registration records. The size of the jury depends on the case. Nine jurors take part when the offence carries a possible death sentence or life imprisonment, and seven in other cases.

When the arguments close, the jurors enter the deliberation room. Only jurors take part in this meeting. If all of them agree, that agreement becomes the verdict. If they do not, they must hear the opinion of the judge who heard the case and then decide by majority. Even then the judge may not state an opinion on guilt or innocence, and may not take part in the verdict itself. The foreperson writes a verdict sheet setting out the number of guilty opinions and the number of not-guilty opinions, collects the signatures of every juror, seals it, and hands it to the bench.

The verdict made in this way does not bind the court. The law states plainly that the verdict and the sentencing opinion of the jurors do not bind the court, which means the judge may hand down a judgment different from the verdict. Yet the law does not stop there. When delivering judgment the presiding judge must tell the defendant what the jurors decided, and when the judgment differs from the verdict, must explain the reason to the defendant.

Placed side by side, these two provisions reveal the design of the system. Had the verdict been made binding, the judgment of the judge would have disappeared. Had it been left as mere reference material, the time the jurors spent would have vanished without a trace. Our system chose the space between. It imposes no duty to follow, but it imposes a duty to explain when not following. Weight is given to the conclusion by explanation rather than by force.

en: A road opens a way for people, but for animals it becomes a wall. A single road across a forest splits a habitat in two. The structure that joins a habitat broken in this way is the eco-corridor. Some pass beneath the road as tunnels, and some go over it as bridges. Korea's first eco-corridor was built in 1998 on a road through Jirisan, and today the national parks hold eighteen of them: nine tunnels and nine bridges.

The Korea National Park Service analysed those eighteen and put the effect into numbers. During the first three years an average of 522 animals a year crossed, and after eight years the figure reached 675, a rise of about thirty percent. At the fifteen corridors more than five years old, roadkill fell by an average of about eighteen percent from before they were built. The tunnel built in 2013 at the Woljeongsa approach road in Odaesan recorded the largest reduction of all, 87.3 percent. This was possible because the corridors were not built alone; guiding fences and signboards were placed alongside them.

What matters most in these figures is not the size of the effect but its timing. Animals do not use an unfamiliar structure at once. The rise in crossings and the fall in accidents came only after several years, and the service treats the point around five years, when use levels off, as the settling stage. Had these corridors been graded right after completion, every one of them would have been recorded as having no effect.

Building them, however, is not enough on its own. The Ministry of Environment surveyed all 564 eco-corridors in the country and then asked for improvements at 535 of them. In more than a few, grass and trees inside had failed to grow, or the passage was shared with drainage channels and farm tracks so that its own function was weakened. Saying a bridge has been built and saying animals cross that bridge are not the same thing.

The direction in which the rules are changing therefore points at checking rather than building. The ministry has decided to strengthen the review of installation plans in advance, to gather corridor information into a single system, and to add a new procedure for evaluating each corridor after it is built. Building brings budgets and opening ceremonies; counting brings neither. Yet without counting, we cannot even know what has gone wrong.

en: The work of archaeology usually begins without knowing exact years. Bowls and ornaments taken from the ground are grouped by similar shape, and only their order is established, that this comes before that. The state of knowing the order but not the year lasts a long time. For this reason a single object that pins down a year can be worth more than all the other objects of its age put together.

In 1971, while a drainage ditch was being dug in Gongju, a tomb built of bricks came to light by chance. Its style showed the influence of the Liang dynasty of southern China. A stone beast stood in the middle of the passage, and in front of it lay two flat stone tablets side by side. They were memorial tablets of blue-grey stone, about 41.5 centimetres by 35, carved in regular script.

The king's tablet recorded that King Sama of Baekje, Great General Yeongdong, died on the seventh day of the fifth month of 523 at the age of sixty-two and was laid in the great tomb on the twelfth day of the eighth month of 525. The queen's tablet recorded that she died in the twelfth month of 526 and was laid to rest on the twelfth day of the second month of 529, once the three-year mourning was over. The back of the queen's tablet was a land-purchase deed: a document stating that on the twelfth day of the eighth month of 525 the ground for the tomb had been bought from the earth god for ten thousand coins. It remains the only such deed found in a tomb of the Three Kingdoms period.

These two stones settled two questions at once. They showed that the owner of the tomb was King Muryeong of Baekje, and they gave the year the tomb was built. The objects found inside therefore gained a fixed time of making as well. A whole set of objects with known dates had appeared. Since then those objects have served as a ruler for judging the age of similar things from other tombs, and are used as reference material for tracing how the tombs and metal craftwork of Baekje changed.

One certain thing puts many uncertain things in order. What makes this tomb exceptional is not that it is the largest or the most splendid, but that those who buried the king wrote down the dates. That ordinary act of leaving a record drove the firmest nail available into the scholarship of fifteen centuries later.

en: The word preservation sounds like leaving something untouched. Letters carved in stone are like that: read fifteen centuries later although no one tended them. With digital records, however, the word turns upside down. Left untouched, they disappear fastest of all.

They vanish along two paths. One is the ageing of the medium. A disk holding a record becomes unreadable as time passes. The other is the disappearance of the format. A file that opened only with a particular program has its contents locked inside the moment that program is gone. The file sits there intact, yet there is no way to get anything out of it.

The National Archives of Korea therefore repeats two conversions. One is media conversion, moving records from an ageing medium onto a new one; the other is format conversion, changing a form that will not last into one that will. In choosing a preservation medium they weigh lifespan and durability, large capacity and low cost, and how widely the medium is used. The format too was chosen by comparing candidates against nine criteria, such as whether it is an open standard, whether it is stable, and whether it can carry descriptive information. The document preservation format settled on in this way is PDF/A, approved as an international standard in 2005 and open for anyone to use without payment.

A new problem arises here. If a record is copied onward again and again, how can anyone say that what remains is the same as what was first made? So when the archives move a record, they keep the original, the converted version and the descriptive information bundled together. At each step, from the producing body to the records office and on to the permanent archives, a fresh electronic signature is attached, proving in an unbroken chain that this is the authentic record.

Keeping preservation media in two sets follows the same logic. The medium that counts as the original is held apart and used as little as possible, while what people handle day to day is a duplicate. Digital preservation, in the end, is not a matter of putting something away. It is a matter of copying it onward and proving each time that it is still the same. A name carved in stone survived without care; a record made today vanishes the moment someone lets go of it.

en: There are several ways to measure a medical book: how many illnesses it covers, how accurate it is, how widely it was read. With Donguibogam one more must be added — the question of whom it took as its reader.

In 1597 King Seonjo ordered the royal physician Heo Jun to gather the medical writings into one. Heo Jun began compiling from the medical books of China and Korea, finished the work in 1610, and had it printed with wooden type at the royal clinic in 1613. It ran to twenty-five volumes in twenty-five books, an encyclopaedic medical work arranged in sections on internal medicine, external forms, miscellaneous diseases, remedies and acupuncture.

The direction of the compilation shows throughout the text. So that people living where physicians and medicines were hard to obtain could treat illness themselves, the remedies in common use at the time were selected; and for the native materials found on Korean soil, the name, the place they grew, the season for gathering them and the way to take them were all recorded. In all 1,403 medicinal materials are listed, and for 637 of them the name is also written in Korean script. Only 102 had to be brought from China, a little over seven percent of the whole.

Set these two figures side by side and the compiler's judgment becomes readable. Writing names in Korean script was a device to let people who knew no Chinese characters find a material; building the book around domestic ingredients was a device to make those materials actually obtainable. A reader must be able to read it and to get hold of it. Take away either one and the book becomes an object that exists but cannot be used.

Donguibogam was inscribed as a UNESCO Memory of the World document in 2009. What was cited was not only the precision of its medical content. Alongside it stood the point that the idea of the state supplying medical care to ordinary people is realised in this book earlier than in any other region of the world. Good knowledge is not enough merely by being correct; it has to reach the people who need it most — and a book four hundred years old showed this first.

en: The long-standing method of printing was the woodblock. A page's worth of characters was carved whole into a board, inked, and pressed onto paper. Carving took great labour, but as long as the board survived the same book could be printed any number of times. Its weakness is plain: to print a different book, the whole board had to be carved again from the start.

Metal type inverted this structure. Each character is cast in metal and kept; only the characters needed for a page are picked out and set, printed, then broken up and reused for the next page. One set of type can handle many kinds of book, which suits printing small numbers of many titles. The labour, in effect, moved from carving the board to making the type in advance.

The oldest book printed this way that still survives is the Jikji. Its formal name is Baegun hwasang chorok buljo jikji simche yojeol, a Buddhist text compiled by the late Goryeo monk Baegun Gyeonghan. The first edition was printed with cast type at Heungdeoksa temple outside Cheongju in 1377, after Gyeonghan's death — seventy-eight years before Gutenberg printed his forty-two-line Bible. At an exhibition in Paris in 1972 it was recognised as the oldest surviving book printed with metal type, and in 2001 it was inscribed as a UNESCO Memory of the World document.

In handling this fact, however, something must be distinguished. That a book was printed at the earliest date and that the technology changed a society are different statements. The Jikji was issued in two volumes, but what survives is the lower volume alone, its first leaf missing, held in the National Library of France. The very fact that a single book remains gives some sense of the scale of printing at the time.

Here lies a trap people often fall into when reading the history of technology. Who came first is a question that can be answered clearly, but what the technology changed is a question that must be weighed against other evidence. The worth of the Jikji does not lie in its ranking alone. It lies in its being physical evidence of how humanity developed the art of printing.

The oldest book printed this way that still survives is the Jikji.
Its formal name is Baegun hwasang chorok buljo jikji simche yojeol,
a Buddhist text compiled by the late Goryeo monk Baegun Gyeonghan.
The first edition was printed with cast type at Heungdeoksa temple outside Cheongju in 1377,
after Gyeonghan's death — seventy-eight years before Gutenberg printed his forty-two-line Bible.
At an exhibition in Paris in 1972 it was recognised as the oldest surviving book printed with metal type,
and in 2001 it was inscribed as a UNESCO Memory of the World document.
That a book was printed at the earliest date
and that the technology changed a society are different statements.
The Jikji was issued in two volumes,
but what survives is the lower volume alone,
held in the National Library of France.
The very fact that a single book remains gives some sense of the scale of printing at the time.
Here lies a trap people often fall into when reading the history of technology.
Who came first is a question that can be answered clearly,
but what the technology changed is a question that must be weighed against other evidence.
The worth of the Jikji does not lie in its ranking alone.
It lies in its being physical evidence of how humanity developed the art of printing.

en: A house is an answer to a climate. In a cold place the task is to hold heat in; in a hot and humid place the task is to let heat and damp out. The two tasks point in opposite directions, so choosing one usually means giving up the other. What makes the hanok remarkable is that it set both inside a single building.

The ondol is the northern answer. Its structure runs from the furnace through the threshold, the flues, the flat stones, the ash pit and the chimney. Heat from the fire crosses the threshold into the flues beneath the floor, warms the stones laid over them, and escapes through the chimney. The threshold spreads the heat evenly while stopping ash from passing into the flues. Heated stone passing warmth to the floor is conduction; heat spreading from the stones through the room is radiation; warmed air circulating up and down is convection.

The maru is the southern answer. Its root is the practice of raising a floor high above the ground to escape damp in hot, humid regions. Frames are jointed lengthwise and crosswise with boards fitted between them, so that air moves beneath the floor. It is a design pointing in exactly the opposite direction from the heat-holding ondol.

It took a long time for the two methods to meet on one level. The daecheong that developed in the south moved northward and the ondol moved southward until at last they met in one house. In winter people live in the ondol room; in summer they live on the open wooden floor of the daecheong. The eaves rest on the same calculation. Their length is set by reckoning the sun's noon altitude, so that midsummer light falls outside the stone platform while winter light reaches into the room.

This house is not the result of pushing a single principle to its limit. It is the result of accepting two conflicting demands in the face of a climate whose summers and winters are both sharp. Had one answer been made to carry all four seasons, some season would surely have been uncomfortable. That is why a form in which ondol and maru coexist in one building is rare in the world.

en: The progress of learning is often told as the achievement of one outstanding person. Yet in some periods an exchange of objections carried on between two people occupies a larger place than any single work. In Korean Neo-Confucianism that place is held by the Four-Seven debate.

It began with a single line. While revising Jeong Jiun's Diagram of the Heavenly Mandate, Yi Hwang wrote that "the four beginnings are issued by principle and the seven feelings by material force", and in 1559 Gi Daeseung sent a letter objecting to it. The four beginnings are four impulses such as pitying others and knowing shame; the seven feelings are seven emotions including joy and anger. As Gi Daeseung saw it, both are equally one feeling, and the four beginnings do not exist apart from the seven.

The debate proceeded by letter rather than by meeting. Yi Hwang was born in 1501 and Gi Daeseung in 1527, twenty-six years apart, yet the younger man raised the problem first and the elder answered with reasons. The letters continued until 1566, and in the course of them Yi Hwang refined his own wording several times. Accepting a correction and altering an expression was treated not as defeat but as a procedure for becoming accurate.

Nor did it close in victory or defeat. In 1566 Gi Daeseung composed two pieces setting out his view and sent them, and Yi Hwang judged their content excellent. With that the debate ended. Rather than one side yielding, it is closer to say that both positions came to rest in a clearer state than before.

What this debate left behind was not a conclusion but a question. Seong Hon and Yi I took the same problem up afterwards, and the arguments passing among the four became the model for later discussion. As most Neo-Confucians of the later Joseon period joined in, the discussion grew vast and finely worked. A well-framed question outlasts any one person's answer, and this debate shows it.

en: As heatwaves grow longer year by year, urban heat has moved from something individuals endure to something a city must manage. But deciding what to fix requires first knowing where it is hot and by how much. Satellites and spatial data have begun to answer that question, which no one can settle by feel alone.

The National Institute of Forest Science analysed the relationship between urban forests and summer land surface temperature across the twenty-five districts of Seoul. Satellite images were laid over the Korea Forest Service's spatial data on urban forests, and district-level indicators were compared with average summer surface temperatures. The result was consistent. The higher a district's canopy cover — the share of the city shaded by tree crowns — the lower its summer surface temperature, and districts with canopy cover above thirty percent showed lower average surface temperatures than those without.

Trees lower temperature in two ways. One is blocking: the shade made by leaves and branches keeps strong solar radiation from reaching the ground. The other is absorbing: transpiration, in which water leaves the foliage as vapour, carries surrounding heat away. Shade reduces the heat coming in while transpiration removes heat already there.

Large forests are not the only ones that work. Thermal camera measurements showed street tree shade lowering temperature by an average of 2.3 to 2.7 degrees, and shade from trees on traffic islands by as much as 4.5 degrees. The larger figure on traffic islands was attributed to tall, leafy trees transpiring vigorously while also blocking direct sunlight. The case of Yeouido is sharper still. In 1996, before the grove was planted, the plaza was on average 2.5 degrees warmer at the surface than its surroundings; by 2015, with the grove established, it was 0.9 degrees cooler.

What this research shows is not the common-sense point that trees are cool. It is that we can now identify, in numbers and on a map, which neighbourhood is hotter and why. Once that can be identified, where to plant first can be decided too. Faced with heat, a city has options beyond enduring it and adding air conditioning.

en: Bundling complicated figures under a few names happens everywhere. School marks are sorted into letters, the strength of an earthquake is called a magnitude, the state of the air is announced as good or bad. Bundling makes judgment faster. In exchange, something is lost at the moment of bundling. The fine dust grades are an example that shows the gain and the loss together.

Consider the subject first. Fine dust means particles ten micrometres across or less, and ultrafine dust 2.5 micrometres or less. Ultrafine particles are about one twentieth to one thirtieth the diameter of a hair, so they are not filtered in the airway but penetrate to the alveoli, and some enter the bloodstream. Short exposure is known to worsen conditions such as asthma attacks, acute bronchitis and irregular heartbeat, while long exposure raises the risk of cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease and lung cancer.

Concentrations are therefore measured and forecast daily. There are four forecast grades for ultrafine dust. Zero to fifteen is good, sixteen to thirty-five moderate, thirty-six to seventy-five bad, seventy-six or above very bad. In addition, an advisory is issued when the hourly average exceeds seventy-five for two hours or more, and an alert when it exceeds one hundred and fifty for two hours or more.

Lay the numbers out and the character of the grades appears. The bad band runs from thirty-six to seventy-five, its ends more than double apart, and very bad has no upper boundary at all. Under one name, the amount reaching the body can be entirely different. The boundaries, moreover, are not lines drawn by nature but divisions set by people to give guidance for behaviour. A rise of one, from thirty-five to thirty-six, changes the name, yet there is no ground for saying that this one does more to the body than the distance from thirty-six to seventy-five.

None of this means the grades are useless. They let a judgment be made in a moment, and they give a standard for action to sensitive groups in particular: children, older people, pregnant women, and those with respiratory or cardiovascular disease. What they should not be read as is a guarantee of safety. A name points at a band; it does not mean that everything below it is harmless. Take direction from the grade and gauge the degree from the number — that is how to use a forecast properly.

en: Most medicines do not lose their effect from long use. A fever reducer will still bring down a fever ten years from now, and a painkiller will still ease pain. Antibiotics are different. The more they are used the less they work, and that change happens not in one person's body but across a whole society.

The cause is natural selection. When an antibiotic is used, bacteria weak against it die and only those that happen to carry a tolerant trait survive. With their competitors gone they breed, and a population on which the drug does not work is formed. These are resistant bacteria. Gut bacteria that resist even carbapenem, a powerful antibiotic, are commonly called superbugs and are a target of control.

This is why countermeasures do not end inside hospitals. The Third National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance, drawn up by the government in 2026, involved seven ministries with the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency in charge. Agriculture, marine, food and environment ministries joined the health side because antibiotics used in livestock and aquaculture, and the resistant bacteria arising there, reach people by way of food and the environment. The plan's national vision is accordingly not confined to humans but covers resistance across people, animals, plants, food and the environment.

The concrete directions are broadly two. One is optimising antibiotic use: expanding the programme that checks whether prescriptions in medical institutions are appropriate, and revising the rules so that in agriculture, livestock and fisheries every antibiotic is used only through a prescription. The other is reducing infection itself. Strengthening infection prevention in medical institutions and widening vaccination lowers how often people fall ill, and with it how often antibiotics are needed.

The nature of this problem is somewhat unusual. For a patient, getting well quickly is a gain; for a livestock farm, raising healthy animals is a gain. Each judgment is, on the whole, reasonable. Yet as those reasonable choices pile up, the shared resource everyone relies on — the effectiveness of the drug — shrinks. Antibiotics show that some resources cannot be saved alone; they are kept only by being saved together.

en: There are two routes by which data made by public bodies is opened to citizens. One is a request for information disclosure, the other is open public data. Both put data out, but they differ in the law behind them, in their purpose, and in the form the data takes.

A disclosure request rests on the Act on Access to Information by Public Institutions. Its purpose is to guarantee the public's right to know and to keep the running of government transparent. Non-electronic material such as paper documents is covered, and no fixed shape is required for what is handed over. The channel is the information disclosure portal. The defining feature of this system is that it moves only when a request is made.

Open public data rests on the Act on Promotion of the Provision and Use of Public Data. Its purpose is different from the start: creating new business and jobs through private use, and raising public convenience, are its stated aims. A condition therefore attaches to the form. Electronic information must be released in a machine-readable form. The channel is the public data portal.

That condition — machine-readable — is the heart of it. Take the same bus timetable: photograph the table and post the image, and a person can read it while a program cannot pull the numbers out. Release it as data in a defined format, and anyone can take it and build an app or a service. Data that changes often, such as live bus arrivals, is opened through what is called an open API.

The effect can be seen in figures. At the end of 2013, the year the public data act took effect, the portal listed 5,272 open datasets; by the end of December 2024 the figure was one hundred thousand, about twenty times as many. Over the same period, the number of times the private sector downloaded data or applied for an open API rose from fourteen thousand to 75.79 million. While openings grew twentyfold, use grew far more. Data is a resource that does not shrink when shared, and grows in worth as more people use it.
